title: Working a flat circle
subtitle: Increase steadily, finish the round, repeat — the circle stays flat instead of cupping
excerpt: A flat crochet circle needs a fixed number of increases per round to stay flat. Too few and the circle cups into a bowl; too many and it ruffles. The standard rule — six per round in double crochet, twelve in treble — keeps the maths predictable.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet in-the-round chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet — the classic doily and mat construction across multiple volumes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of stitches added per round. To keep a circle flat, the increase rate stays fixed each round (6 per round for double crochet circles, 12 per round for treble circles).

heroPrompt: A flat crochet circle of about 15 cm diameter in cream DK cotton, six rounds worked, photographed flat from above on a pale linen background — the circle lies perfectly flat with no cupping or ruffling, the round boundaries faintly visible.

content.text: A flat crochet circle needs a fixed number of increases per round. Too few and the circle cups into a bowl shape; too many and it ruffles at the edge. The geometry is the same as a paper disc — the circumference grows by a fixed amount each round, and so does the stitch count.

The standard rules: six new stitches per round in double crochet, eight per round in half treble, twelve per round in treble. Round 1 holds the base stitch count; every subsequent round adds the same number, distributed evenly. The shape stays flat as long as you don't break the pattern.

attrs.title: Why these numbers
attrs.body: The maths comes from the height of each stitch relative to its width. Double crochet is about as tall as it is wide — six increases per round matches the circumference growth. Treble is twice as tall, so the circle has to widen twice as fast — twelve increases per round. Use any other number and the circle goes wrong predictably.

content.text: Start with a magic ring (or a chain-4 ring closed with a slip stitch if you prefer). The example below uses the magic ring; the maths is the same either way.
Round 1: into the magic ring, ch 3 (counts as the first tr), 11 tr into the ring. Sl st to top of beg ch-3 to join. (12 sts.) Pull the magic ring tail to close the centre.
Round 2: ch 3 (counts as first tr), 1 tr in same st as join. *2 tr in next st; repeat from * around. Sl st to top of beg ch-3 to join. (24 sts.)
Round 3: ch 3 (counts as first tr), 1 tr in same st as join. *1 tr in next st, 2 tr in next st; repeat from * around. Sl st to top of beg ch-3. (36 sts.)
Round 4: ch 3 (counts as first tr), 1 tr in same st. *1 tr in next 2 sts, 2 tr in next st; repeat from * around. Sl st to top of beg ch-3. (48 sts.)

Each subsequent round adds one more plain stitch between each increase. Round 5 has the increase every 4 sts; round 6 every 5 sts; round 7 every 6 sts. Twelve more stitches per round, evenly spaced. Continue to the size you want.

attrs.heading: When the circle doesn't lie flat
attrs.intro: Four common flat-circle problems and the fix for each.

items.symptom: The circle cups into a shallow bowl shape
items.cause: Not enough increases. Either you missed a 2 tr increase somewhere, or you're working trebles with a 10-per-round increase rate.
items.fix: Count the stitches at the end of each round. The count should match the formula (round 2 has 24, round 3 has 36, round 4 has 48, etc.). If a count is short, you missed an increase. Add the missing stitch in the same place on the next round.

items.symptom: The edge of the circle ruffles
items.cause: Too many increases. Either you added an extra 2 tr increase somewhere, or you're using too many increases for the stitch height (e.g. 12 per round in double crochet).
items.fix: Count the stitches at the end of each round. If the count is over the formula, work fewer increases in the next round to compensate.

items.symptom: The join lines up as a visible diagonal stripe
items.cause: Every round starts the increases in the same stitch as the previous round.
items.fix: Stagger the increases. Round 4 can start its first increase one stitch further along than round 3. The diagonal will fade.

items.symptom: The centre has a visible hole even with a magic ring
items.cause: The magic ring wasn't pulled tight before round 2.
items.fix: Pull the magic ring tail firmly before continuing. If the centre is still loose, sew the tail through the round 1 stitches with a tapestry needle and then pull tight.

content.text: A flat treble circle of six rounds in DK cotton makes a coaster; eight rounds makes a placemat; twelve rounds is the start of a small mat. For amigurumi and round bag bases, the same maths in double crochet (six increases per round) gives a tighter circle that holds a bowl shape when you stop increasing. From there, hexagons and granny squares use the same in-the-round logic — they're flat shapes with the increase concentrated at the corners.
